image_description:
## 1) Chart type
A **faceted range/bar chart** (small multiples) showing **daily high–low temperature ranges** for multiple cities across a 10-day period, with actual vs forecast values distinguished by color.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Small multiples / faceting** by **city**: each city has its own mini-panel.
- Within each panel, temperatures are shown as **vertical range bars** for each day.
- **Color/lightness** distinguishes **actual** vs **forecast** and also highlights the **normal range** in the background.
- No stacking is used.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate small-multiple panels; panel title |
| Date / Day | Temporal | Position along x-axis within each panel; day-of-week labels (T, W, T, F, S, S, M, T, W, T) |
| Daily high temperature | Quantitative | Upper endpoint / top of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Daily low temperature | Quantitative | Lower endpoint / bottom of vertical temperature range bar on y-axis |
| Temperature (degrees) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis; axis labels such as 20°, 40°, 60°, 80° |
| Actual vs Forecast status | Categorical/nominal | Color/lightness of range bars (darker for actual, medium gray for forecast) |
| Normal temperature range | Quantitative | Light gray background vertical range band behind each day’s bar |
| Record high / record low range | Quantitative | Very light gray outer vertical range band shown in legend/explanation |

I notice first in these graphs that each color represents something different, whether it be a record, a current finding, or a prediction. It is obvious that southern states have drastically higher temperatures than northern cities this time of year. In a lot of these cities, people are experiencing drastic temperature fluctuations.  Atlanta, Boston, Minneapolis, and New York are all cities that experienced 30-degree differences in just five days. In other cities, temperatures are not near the expected temperatures, but rather near the record highs and lows. Cities like Dallas, Fort Myers, Orlando, and Tampa all reached temperatures above the normal high. More rare were cities dipping below their normal lows, but it did happen briefly in Denver and Minneapolis.
What I am most curious about in this graph is the cause for such drastic fluctuations in weather and why many cities are experiencing extreme highs and lows in temperature. This is likely in part due to global warming. I am also curious if the cities whose forecasts were rather drastic reached their predicted temperatures. 
This relates to me and my community because we have been experiencing drastic weather ourselves. Here, the weather was nearing zero degrees last week, but just days later it neared 50 degrees. 
A catchphrase for this graph is "Wacky Weather Sweeps the Nation".

The light gray bars of the graph show the average temperature in past years during this time. Particularly cities on the east coast saw higher than the average temperatures. Cities in the northeast, like Boston that are generally colder, recorded temperatures over 40 degrees for Dec. 6-10. While cities on the west coast experienced lower than the average temperature recorded. 

I wonder if the predicted forecasts were accurate and if they followed similar trends to Dec. 6-10. I also wonder the connections to climate change and global warming. 

This affects my community because I live in New Jersey, which is on the East Coast. New Jersey generally has colder winters, but the weather has been generally warmer, in the 50s and 60s. The lack of snow this season makes me concerned about the affects of global warming on my community.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the majority of places in the country had temperatures higher than normal for the time of the year. For example, on December 6-7 in New York, there were near-record high temperatures for the month of December. Also, at the end of the 10 days in Minneapolis, the forecast was higher than average temperatures, despite Minneapolis being a very cold city in December. I also notice a great amount of fluctuation between the cities. This has to do with the geographical climate of the areas, such as Boston, having colder temperatures than Miami because it is further north. I wonder why some places have greater fluctuation than others. Ft. Meyers has a fairly even temperature and predicted temperature over the 4 days, but Atlantas change greatly. I wonder how climate change and global warming play a role in the warm temperatures many places have been experiencing. The information in this graph affects me because I live in an area experiencing above-normal temperatures for this time of the year. I am also concerned about global warming and how that affects my life and my environment. My headline is "Changing City Temperatures."

1. What do you notice? I notice that 22 cities have graphs showing their temperature from December 6th to December 15th. Each day has a range from low to high temperatures. I notice that the independent variable is the days in the period (categorical). The dependent variable is the temperature (quantitative).

2. What do you wonder? I wonder why cities in Texas have varying temperatures throughout the 10 days, but cities in Florida have consistent temperatures. 

3. What impact does this have on you and your community? Global warming/climate change is a serious topic covered in our world today. For a cold month like December, the temperatures in America sometimes seem to be a little too high. Boston, for example, is a city that typically has very low temperatures in the winter. However, during the 10-day period, there were times when the temperature almost reached 60°F. Global warming could be a reason behind this.

 4. What's going on in this graph? Throughout the 10 days, Miami, Orlando, Tampa, Ft. Myers, and other cities in America (usually southern) have temperatures that remain consistent. On the other hand, New York, Boston, Minneapolis, Washington, and other cities have fluctuating temperatures.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs display the 10-day temperature trends (Dec. 6 – 15) for 22 U.S. cities as provided by AccuWeather.  Note the explanation of the graph in the top left corner.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, how about a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. We look forward to replying to your discoveries.

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included these graphs.  

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, Jan. 6 with moderation on Wednesday, Jan. 11.  Have a good holiday season.
